scenarioName: Motorcycle Crash — Severe TBI with Developing Cushing's Triad

scenarioStory.history: 35-year-old male lost control of his motorcycle on a curve and was ejected without a helmet, striking his head directly on the pavement. Bystanders report a brief loss of consciousness followed by confusion and repetitive questioning. He vomited once at the scene and has become progressively harder to arouse since bystanders called 911.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: Crew arrives to find a 35-year-old male ejected from his motorcycle without a helmet, lying in the roadside ditch. He is confused, repeating the same questions, and combative with examination, with an actively oozing scalp laceration. → Primary survey and O2 given: Crew completes a MARCH primary survey with cervical stabilization maintained, applies high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask, and begins trending neurologic status given the mechanism and moderate head injury presentation. → Cushing's triad recognized, RSI performed: The patient's GCS declines to 6 with a dilating, sluggish right pupil, rising blood pressure to 172/98, falling heart rate to 46, and irregular respirations — Cushing's triad indicating rising intracranial pressure. He can no longer protect his airway, meeting criteria for RSI with head-injury-specific ventilation targets. → Tube confirmed, ventilated per head-injury targets: The endotracheal tube is confirmed with waveform capnography and secured. Ventilation is titrated to avoid hyperventilation and hypocapnia, and fluids are given to maintain blood pressure above the head-injury threshold while transporting to the highest level trauma center.

patientInformation.patientCondition: Unhelmeted motorcycle crash with head trauma

scenarioEvents.name: Initial Contact
scenarioEvents.description: Crew arrives to find a 35-year-old male ejected from his motorcycle without a helmet, lying in the roadside ditch. He is confused, repeating the same questions, and combative with examination, with an actively oozing scalp laceration.

scenarioEvents.name: Primary survey and O2 given
scenarioEvents.description: Crew completes a MARCH primary survey with cervical stabilization maintained, applies high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask, and begins trending neurologic status given the mechanism and moderate head injury presentation.
relatedChecklist: Maintain cervical stabilization while performing MARCH primary survey
Apply high-flow O2 via non-rebreather as precaution against deterioration
Perform serial GCS/AVPU checks; reassess pupils with any change in mentation

scenarioEvents.name: Cushing's triad recognized, RSI performed
scenarioEvents.description: The patient's GCS declines to 6 with a dilating, sluggish right pupil, rising blood pressure to 172/98, falling heart rate to 46, and irregular respirations — Cushing's triad indicating rising intracranial pressure. He can no longer protect his airway, meeting criteria for RSI with head-injury-specific ventilation targets.
relatedChecklist: Preoxygenate with high-flow O2/BVM for at least 2 minutes prior to RSI
Fentanyl 86 mcg IV pretreatment (86 kg × 1 mcg/kg), 2-3 min before intubation
Etomidate 21.5 mg IV induction (86 kg × 0.25 mg/kg)
Rocuronium 86 mg IV paralytic (86 kg × 1 mg/kg)
Intubate with 8.0 ETT; confirm placement with waveform capnography

scenarioEvents.name: Tube confirmed, ventilated per head-injury targets
scenarioEvents.description: The endotracheal tube is confirmed with waveform capnography and secured. Ventilation is titrated to avoid hyperventilation and hypocapnia, and fluids are given to maintain blood pressure above the head-injury threshold while transporting to the highest level trauma center.
relatedChecklist: Ventilate at 10 breaths/min targeting EtCO2 35-45 mmHg; avoid hyperventilation
NS bolus to maintain SBP ≥110 mmHg; do not wait for hypotension to develop
Transport to highest level trauma center per severe head injury criteria

scenarioEvents.name: RSI without pre-O2
scenarioEvents.description: Crew proceeds directly to sedation and paralysis without the minimum two-minute preoxygenation period. The patient desaturates rapidly during the intubation attempt, developing hypoxic bradycardia.
relatedChecklist: Stop the intubation attempt; resume BVM with high-flow O2 to recover SpO2 before re-attempting
